title: The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities
research_question: How does the supply of road infrastructure in metropolitan areas affect the amount of vehicle travel? Specifically, does expanding lane kilometers of highways and major urban roads reduce congestion, or does it generate proportional increases in driving, and through what channels (individual behavior, commercial traffic, migration, traffic diversion) does any such response operate? Additionally, does the provision of public transit reduce overall vehicle travel?
data_description: The unit of observation is the US Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) drawn to 1999 boundaries, with 228 MSAs covered. Road and traffic data come from the US Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS) Universe and Sample files for 1983, 1993, and 2003, providing lane kilometers, average annual daily traffic (AADT), vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT), and truck shares for interstate highways and major urban roads, distinguishing urbanized from non-urbanized portions of MSAs. Individual and household travel behavior (commute distance/time, daily and annual household VKT) is taken from the 1995 and 2001 National Personal Transportation Survey (NPTS) using confidential geocodes. Public transit is measured by daily peak-service large buses from Section 15 reports for 1984, 1994, and 2004. Additional data include MSA population, sectoral employment (County Business Patterns), socioeconomic and demographic characteristics, and physical geography (elevation, ruggedness, climate, sprawl).
institutional_context: American households spend large amounts of time commuting and routine travel time grew roughly 10% between 1995 and 2001, generating substantial congestion costs and a third of US carbon emissions from energy use. Policy debates pit road builders, who argue that adding highway capacity relieves congestion, against transit advocates, who argue that without new transit highways will become unusable. The interstate highway system was largely shaped by the 1947 federal interstate plan, designed to connect principal metropolitan and industrial centers and serve national defense, and was built out over subsequent decades. Earlier transportation networks—1898 railroad routes built by private companies during the industrial revolution and routes of major US exploration expeditions between 1835 and 1850—shaped the corridors along which later roads were laid. Federal involvement in public transit expanded sharply with the 1970 Urban Mass Transportation Act and the 1974 National Mass Transportation Act, transforming transit into a heavily subsidized quasi-public sector with persistent funding patterns across cities.
